name: 1 Thessalonians
author: The letter names Paul, along with his travelling companions Silvanus (also called Silas) and Timothy, and it is almost universally accepted as Paul's own. Paul was a Jew from Tarsus, in what is now southern Turkey, trained as a Pharisee, a member of a Jewish group devoted to strictly keeping God's law. He once persecuted followers of Jesus, then became one of the movement's leading missionaries, earning his living as a tentmaker as he travelled. This is probably one of his earliest surviving letters, and perhaps the oldest writing in the New Testament.
audience: It was written to a young church in Thessalonica, a busy port city and the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia in northern Greece. Most believers there seem to have been non-Jews who had recently turned away from worshipping idols. Paul had been forced to leave the city after only a short stay because of opposition, and the new believers were facing pressure and hostility from their neighbours.
era: The letter was probably written around AD 50–51, during the reign of the emperor Claudius, likely from Corinth in southern Greece. Thessalonica sat on the Via Egnatia, a major Roman road, and was full of traders, temples to many gods, and honours paid to the emperor. Small groups meeting in homes to worship Jesus stood out in such a city and could easily draw suspicion.

notes.1:1: Silvanus is the Silas who travelled with Paul in the book of Acts; Timothy was a younger co-worker. Both had helped found the church in Thessalonica.
notes.1:2: News of the Thessalonians' new faith had spread through Macedonia and Achaia, the Roman provinces covering northern and southern Greece.
notes.2:1: Paul arrived after being beaten and jailed in Philippi, and travelling speakers who sought money and praise were common, so he recalls working to support himself.
notes.2:13: The believers were suffering at the hands of their own townspeople; a minority of scholars think part of this section was added later, though most accept it as Paul's.
notes.2:17: After being forced out of Thessalonica, Paul went on to Athens and, anxious for the church, sent Timothy back from there to strengthen them.
notes.3:6: Timothy had just rejoined Paul, likely in Corinth, bringing an encouraging report about the church; this news seems to have prompted the letter.
notes.4:1: These converts came from a Greek and Roman culture where sexual relationships outside marriage, especially for men, were widely tolerated.
notes.4:9: Many Greeks looked down on manual labour, and it seems some in the church had stopped working and were relying on others.
notes.4:13: Some believers had died since Paul left, and the church was troubled about what this meant for them when Jesus returned.
notes.5:23: Letters like this were read aloud to the whole congregation gathered together, often in someone's home.
